content.thinking:
I'm sketching the elephant's proportions based on a real African bush elephant—shoulder height around 3.3m, body length, ear and trunk sizing—and working out coordinates for the body facing forward.

Now I'm planning the skeleton rig: a hip root with a spine chain to chest, neck, and head, plus a tail chain, four legs with mostly straight limb IK (front legs straighter, hind legs with slight knee bend), toenails on the feet, a seven-joint trunk curling forward with a finger tip, hinged ear slabs, curved tusk sweeps, and a separate jaw joint. I'm also deciding to use low-poly faceted shading with flat sections rather than smooth surfaces.

For color, I'm settling on a gray-brown elephant skin palette with darker shading tones, a lighter belly, pinkish inner ears, ivory tusks, pale nails, dark eyes, and dusty mud tones on the lower legs. I'm planning to add subtle mottling and wrinkle texture through paint rather than relying purely on flat polygon colors, keeping it restrained to stay consistent with the low-poly style.

Now I'm working out the body's spatial layout -- ground plane, foot and leg proportions, hip and shoulder joint positions, and a series of cross-section stations defining the torso's width and height from rump to chest.

I'm laying out a spine chain from pelvis through chest to neck, with named joints (pelvis, spine1, spine2, chest, neck) leading to a head joint, which drives the body loft path separately from the station-based catmull curve.

For limbs, I'm attaching leg chains as children of the spine joint with IK, starting the leg tubes embedded inside the body at the hip socket so they blend smoothly with the body's half-width, and I'm considering adding capsule masses at the thigh/shoulder joints for bulk.

I'm working out the front leg joint positions and segment lengths, placing shoulder, elbow, and wrist points so the limb reaches down to a foot near ground level while keeping total segment length roughly matching the hip-to-foot distance.

Still too much sag with simple two-bone IK, so I'll switch to defining the front leg as an explicit chain of points (shoulder, elbow, carpus, foot) run through a catmull path for a more natural curved limb shape.

I'm sketching the foot as a low-poly cylinder pad with front nails attached to the chain's tip joint, then working out hind leg points with the hip-knee-lower leg geometry angling forward then back.

Now I'm placing the sole flush with the floor and adding a toenail ring where the foot disc slightly overhangs the leg radius, then moving on to the head shape -- a domed skull positioned above and forward of the chest, connecting via the neck.

Working out the head loft stations: tracing from the neck base up to the skull dome, adjusting widths and heights at each cross-section so the forehead peaks around shoulder height while the jaw/trunk base sits lower near the face front.

Checking overall scale now: comparing body length (rump to face) against typical bull elephant proportions (body length roughly 6-7.5m including trunk, shoulder height ~3.2m) to see if my length-to-height ratio looks realistic.

Adjusting the rump position back to -2.1 and setting hip/leg positions with proper spacing (~2.1m between hind and front legs) to match real elephant proportions.

Now I'm planning the skeleton structure, starting with a root hip joint and building a spine chain from pelvis to neck base.

I'll use a bone list of [hips, spine] so the loft segments behind hips get attributed to the hips bone region. For the neck, I'm planning a short thick chain from the upper spine to the head joint, with a neck chain named ["neck1","neck2"] running through a few path points before reaching the head position, while the head loft itself rides along the head bone.

Now I'm working through how the spine chain connects into the hips joint, deciding whether the hips and spine1 should coincide at the same position or whether to treat hips as a separate root with its own named joint, settling on keeping "hips" as the root and letting the spine chain start from that same location for simplicity.

I'm also thinking through how the neck chain should parent to the tip of the spine chain, and how the body loft and head loft should bridge near the neck -- making the body loft extend slightly into the neck area while the head loft starts inward so the rigid head mass covers the seam, with the head joint placed around (0, 2.65, 1.9).

For the neck chain itself, I'm settling on naming it so the final joint is literally "head," positioned at the tip of the neck path and aimed along the end tangent, with the chain's role set to "neck." Then I'm planning a separate trunk chain rooted at a face position near (0, 2.35, 2.45) that will path downward from the head.

For the trunk, I'm thinking of a gentle S-curve hanging down and curling forward so the tip ends near the ground, around 2.4 meters long, tapering from roughly 0.3 to 0.12 in radius. I want to add wrinkle rings along the trunk surface using a periodic pattern based on position, considering either painted shading bands or thin torus-like geometric rings for the texture.

I'll build the trunk as a chain of eight joints with a "tentacle" role, then add the finger-like features at the tip — the characteristic upper and lower lobes elephants have — plus a dark disc for the nostril opening facing down and forward at the very end.

Now I'm working out the mouth: a small U-shaped lower jaw hinged beneath the trunk base, extending forward with a pale lip tone against darker surrounding skin, and setting up tusk sockets emerging symmetrically on either side of the trunk base where the actual tusks will attach.

Plotting tusk curvature next, running each one forward-down then sweeping up and outward in a few control points, checking that they clear the trunk's position as it narrows, tapering the radius to a sharp point and giving the base a subtle darker ivory ring near where it meets the skin.

Now I'm shaping the ears as large African-style silhouettes, roughly 1.3 by 1.2 meters, attaching them at the sides of the head with a slight outward flare, and figuring out the extrusion plane and orientation to get them resting naturally against the skull.

Still shaping the ear outline...

I'm giving the ear thickness and bevel on the rolled leading edge, adding rim shading and a radial vein pattern using noise-based painting, plus a small tattered notch along the margin. Then I'm setting up the ear as a two-joint hinge chain attaching at the head for the root and tip bones.

Making the ear flap by rotating about its own vertical axis instead, simplifying the hinge logic. For the eyes, I'm placing small dark spheres at the sides of the head with an amber iris ring and highlight, plus brow ridge arcs and a thin ring of small spikes for lashes to capture that elephant look at low poly.

Positioning the eyes by casting a ray inward from outside the head surface to find the correct attachment point, then sticking the eye geometry onto that hit. I'm also adding a subtle dark streak below the eye along the cheek to suggest a temporal gland mark, blending it into the head paint logic based on distance from the eye position, then moving on to forehead bumps and cheek details.

For body texture, I'm considering sparse hair tufts on the head and tail along with eyelashes and chin whiskers, plus a crackled, cell-based wrinkle pattern for the skin to achieve a hand-painted, low-poly look rather than simple stripes.

Combining a mottled gray base with a slightly darker-edged scale/crackle pattern should give that dry elephant-skin texture, and I want to layer in a dusty red-brown gradient fading in near the lower legs.

Checking texel density, I estimate a 2048 paint sheet gives enough resolution for wrinkle detail, though a 4096 atlas would be even crisper—2048 should suffice for this low-poly style. Now I'm figuring out toenails: elephants have 5 on front feet and 4 on hind, so I'm placing small wedge shapes around the front rim of each foot using an angular ring positioned toward the front-facing direction.

Placing nail geometry... the tricky part is that the tip joint has no child, so its bone has zero length, meaning I need to figure out which bone the nail geometry should actually attach to for correct orientation.

I'll switch to computing positions manually with trig instead, specifying explicit bone, position, and direction for each part. For the footpad, I'm sizing a flattened cylinder with slightly different top and bottom radii, then adding nail boxes arranged along the front arc.

Now I'm planning the tail as a chain of joints hanging down from the rump, tapering in radius toward the tip, with a tuft of dark spikes arranged in a ring at the end.

Computing explicit per-spike directions manually instead of relying on ring tilt, looping over angles to build normalized vectors for each tail-tip spike. Then I'm planning the rest of the hair placement: small dark tufts on the crown, lashes around the eyes, chin whiskers, and sparse scattered tiny spikes across the back using surface scatter for texture.

For broader body hair I'm thinking cards rather than individual spike parts would be far cheaper on the part budget, using a strand texture so one card batch covers hundreds of hairs concentrated more densely on the crown, tail tip, chin, and trunk. I'm also weighing adding small wrinkle ridge geometry at leg joints like knees and elbows to sell skin folds, keeping it minimal given the low-poly style.

Setting ridges at wider radius with closed catmull loops for smooth flat-shaded rings along the trunk.

For the body, I'm adding subtler anatomical features—hip bone bumps, shoulder bumps, and belly curvature—by varying the loft stations' width and height along a spine path, using the back dip between shoulders and raised hips to get a convincing elephant silhouette.

Continuing the remaining stations through the shoulder, chest, and head regions, keeping top/bottom/width consistent so the belly stays around 1.3-1.4 clearance, and planning to run a Catmull-Rom spline through these points for smooth transitions.

For bone assignment, I'm deciding to fold the neck chain into the main body loft, skinning from hips through spine to neck, so the head joint caps the tip while the neck joints handle the intermediate curvature naturally within the same skinned mesh.

The tail gets its own separate sweep, attaching near the rear of the body loft at a specific joint position, while I'm also noting subtle surface details like rib lines and rump sagging for the paint pass rather than geometry.

Now I'm laying out head loft stations as cross-sections (z position with top/bottom/width values) to define the skull shape, treating the head as rigid on its own bone while letting it overlap slightly with the neck for a smooth transition.

I'm checking proportions against real elephant anatomy — reconsidering head height and dome position relative to the shoulder since my initial numbers made it too tall — and deciding the body should use a low-poly faceted look with 8-sided cross-sections and flat shading across body, head, legs, and trunk for a consistent stylized aesthetic.

For finer details I'll skip zygomatic cheek bumps and tail/genital geometry for now to keep things simple, adding them later if needed after a first look. I'm working out the jaw structure as a small box positioned beneath the trunk base, sized to fit within the head loft's lower boundary, with the tusks attached separately to the upper jaw region of the head.

Positioning the jaw box with a center around y=1.78, z=2.15, keeping it narrow and shallow so it reads as a rounded lower lip just under the trunk root, like real elephant anatomy. I'll give it a slightly pale lower-lip tone and keep the mouth closed with no visible seam or tongue detail to avoid unnecessary complexity.

Now I'm moving to the implementation itself, defining skin paint using mottling and cracking functions with specific size, seed, and contrast parameters, and checking the helper signatures in the paint module to get the width and grain parameters right before writing the texture code.
